I propose replacing coarse caller-SCC invalidation with versioned delta propagation over escaped-object closures, using wildcard heap slots for provenance-losing casts.

That proposes a more selective update mechanism while retaining a conservative treatment of casts that lose provenance under the documented IR semantics. Instead of invalidating a caller SCC as a whole merely because some escape-related input changed, versioned deltas would convey changes in escaped-object closure information to dependent reasoning. Wildcard heap slots would stand for heap-slot possibilities that a provenance-losing cast prevents the analysis from identifying precisely. This is a proposal, not an established soundness, answer-equivalence, or latency result.
What does ‘replace coarse caller-SCC invalidation’ mean without specifying an algorithm?

It means proposing not to treat every relevant change as a reason to discard all cached caller-SCC information at the same coarse granularity. Instead, changes to escaped-object closures would be propagated as versioned deltas. The proposal does not say that SCCs cease to matter, that recursive dependencies vanish, or that no caller information is ever recomputed. It changes the proposed granularity of update, subject to preserving soundness and post-edit agreement with full recomputation.
Is a delta just a newer version number?

Not quite. A version distinguishes closure information used at one point from information at another. A delta, conceptually, describes what changed between them. The proposal names both so dependent reasoning could respond to the relevant change rather than only learning that an entire closure has a newer version. It does not specify a delta format, how versions are assigned, or what facts are included.
What changes might a closure delta have to describe?

At a general level, it would need to represent changes in escaped-object closure information that matter to dependent alias answers. That could include a newly relevant or no-longer-relevant abstract heap target, if the documented semantics and the analysis permit that change. The proposal itself does not enumerate delta kinds or say that membership changes capture every relevant change in reachable heap contents or call-target information.
Why is that distinction between closure membership and contents important?

An object can remain reachable through an escaped-object closure while information in one of its heap slots changes. A proposal to propagate closure deltas does not, by its name alone, guarantee that a changed function pointer stored in that slot will be noticed. To preserve alias answers, any relevant dependency on slot contents or resulting indirect-call targets must also be accounted for. This proposal does not specify exactly how those other changes are represented.
Could the delta be propagated only to callers that used a previously listed escaped object?

That restriction would need justification. A changed closure can make an object newly relevant, in which case it may be absent from a list of objects previously used by a caller. The conceptual advantage of propagating closure changes is that dependencies can concern the information determining possible targets, not just an old enumeration of them. The proposal still needs a sound account of which dependent reasoning receives a delta; it does not provide that account in detail.
Does delta propagation automatically tell us which caller summaries change?

No. Receiving a relevant delta signals that information used by a caller may need reconsideration. The caller's resulting alias-relevant information might change or remain the same. Passing changes onward to transitive callers must depend on the information they use, not simply on the fact that a version advanced somewhere. The proposal does not state a particular stopping rule.
And what if there is a recursive SCC among the dependent functions?

Cyclic dependencies still need consistent treatment. A delta reaching one function in a recursive SCC could affect information used by another member and eventually feed back. Replacing coarse caller-SCC invalidation does not authorize treating the members as independent or stopping after one traversal of the cycle. The proposal leaves the specific method of handling those cyclic dependencies open.
Is this a proposal to dispense with function summaries?

No. It proposes a way of updating information when escaped-object closures change. Interprocedural alias reasoning can still rely on function summaries, including summaries with cyclic dependencies. What changes is the suggested response to a relevant closure change, not the requirement to represent and propagate alias-relevant function behavior.
What makes a cast ‘provenance-losing’ in this proposal?

The documented IR semantics would have to say that a particular cast loses the provenance needed to associate its result with a precise prior pointer or heap slot. The proposal names a treatment for casts with that property; it does not decide which cast operations have it. A cast cannot be classified as provenance-losing merely because its syntax looks complicated.
Does a pointer–integer cast always fall into that category?

No universal classification follows. The IR's pointer–integer provenance rules determine what relationships survive any given conversion, including any conditions on a conversion back to a pointer. Wildcard heap slots are proposed for provenance-losing casts, not automatically for every pointer–integer conversion.
Why introduce a wildcard heap slot?

If a cast loses the information needed to name a particular heap slot, a wildcard slot can conservatively represent relevant slot possibilities rather than treating that lost precision as evidence that no heap alias exists. It is an abstraction for uncertainty about heap-slot identity. The proposal does not define which slots the wildcard encompasses or how it interacts with named allocation-site slots; those relationships must be made sound under the documented IR semantics.
Would ‘wildcard’ mean the pointer definitely aliases every heap slot?

No. A may-alias abstraction can retain several possible slots without claiming the pointer actually aliases all of them in every execution. The wildcard's required scope depends on what the provenance-losing cast permits and what the analysis can still distinguish. Its name alone neither proves that every heap slot is possible nor justifies excluding one that remains possible.
Could the wildcard be declared disjoint from all named allocation-site slots?

Not without semantic justification. If the cast result may refer to a heap slot represented by a named allocation site, declaring a wildcard slot definitely separate from that slot would exclude a permitted alias. The proposal would need to define how wildcard and named-slot possibilities relate, rather than using ‘wildcard’ as another word for fresh or disjoint.
Is the external-unknown heap node the same as a wildcard heap slot?

The names describe different conceptual uncertainties. An external-unknown heap node concerns a possible heap object relevant to an opaque return. A wildcard heap slot concerns uncertainty about which slot may be accessed after a provenance-losing cast. An object can have slots, so their effects might interact, but the proposal does not merge the two abstractions or specify their exact relationships.
How would wildcard slots matter to an indirect call?

If a function pointer used for an indirect call can be obtained from a slot reached through a provenance-losing cast, the analysis must account for possible callees allowed by that uncertain slot access. Treating the slot as definitely unrelated to stored function pointers could omit a callee. The proposal does not specify a target-expansion rule for wildcard slots or say every cast result can reach a function pointer.
Could a wildcard make new callees relevant even when a closure's set of escaped objects is unchanged?

Conceptually, yes: uncertainty about which slot is accessed and the possible function pointers stored there are not identical to membership in an escaped-object closure. If either kind of information changes in a way that affects call targets, the appropriate dependencies must be updated. Versioned closure deltas alone do not, without further specification, establish that every such slot or target change is tracked.
Does the proposal prescribe a dependency between the wildcard slot and every caller?

No. The wildcard must conservatively cover slot possibilities relevant under the documented semantics, and callers that depend on the resulting alias or call-target information cannot be left with stale answers. But the proposal does not state that every caller is affected by every wildcard slot or define the dependency representation. Overly narrow dependencies risk missed updates; assuming every caller depends on it would add an unprovided rule.
How could closure deltas and wildcard slots interact in principle?

A change in escaped-object information may change which heap objects are relevant to an opaque return or another escaping pointer path. If such a path goes through a provenance-losing cast, a wildcard slot may be needed to retain permitted access to heap-slot information whose precise identity is unavailable. Dependent alias or call-target reasoning must then respond to the relevant changes. This is a conditional interaction, not a description of a specified edit or a completed implementation.
Could using a wildcard avoid any need to propagate deltas?

Not necessarily. A wildcard expresses uncertainty about slot identity; it does not make cached summaries automatically responsive to changes in escaped-object information. Conversely, propagating a delta does not repair a semantic omission if the wildcard fails to include a permitted slot. The proposal has two complementary pieces: representing uncertain heap access and updating dependent information when the closure changes.
Does making the wildcard very broad automatically satisfy the goal?

No. A broad may-alias representation might avoid some unsound exclusions, but the goal also requires incremental alias answers after single-function edits to match full recomputation's answers. Moreover, the analysis still has to handle the documented IR semantics rather than rely on an undefined interpretation of ‘wildcard.’ The 50% median analysis-latency target remains separate as well.
If a closure loses a possible object, is that a delta worth propagating?

If the loss can affect a dependent alias answer, yes, conceptually. Retaining an old possible target in cached incremental information may remain conservative but differ from full recomputation on the edited program. The proposal does not limit versioned deltas to additions, and any treatment of removals has to respect the semantics and the full-recomputation comparison.
Does a changed closure always justify invalidating the whole caller SCC?

The proposal is specifically to replace coarse caller-SCC invalidation with versioned delta propagation, so it does not posit whole-SCC invalidation as the automatic response to every change. Yet a recursive SCC may still require reconsideration of mutually dependent information when a relevant delta reaches it. The proposed granularity of propagation is not a promise that no SCC will ever be revisited as a unit.
What would make skipping part of a caller SCC unsafe?

If the skipped information depends, directly or through a cycle, on the changed closure or on a heap-slot alias exposed by a provenance-losing cast, leaving it cached could produce a stale answer. A selective update must account for those dependencies before concluding that a portion of the SCC is unaffected. Delta propagation is an approach to making that distinction; its name alone does not prove the dependencies are complete.
Is the proposal claiming a particular reduction in recomputation or latency?

No numerical reduction is reported or predicted in this proposal. Replacing coarse invalidation may reduce unnecessary work, but propagating deltas and accounting for wildcard heap slots also has costs. Whether the approach reaches the broader goal of reducing median analysis latency by 50% while matching full recomputation needs separate evaluation.
Can we already say it preserves soundness for opaque calls and heap objects?

Not yet. The proposal gives candidate mechanisms for closure updates and provenance-losing casts. Soundness still depends on whether opaque-return possibilities, heap targets, casts, and any relevant read, write, or escape effects are represented consistently with the documented IR semantics. Neither a proposed wildcard nor versioning constitutes a semantic proof.
What does full-recompute parity require if we adopt this finer update mechanism?

After a single-function edit, the incremental run must produce the same alias answers as full recomputation on that edited program. A versioned delta must reach every dependent answer that would change, including dependencies made newly relevant through escaped objects or uncertain heap slots. It must also avoid leaving stale possibilities when the full recomputation would no longer include them. That states the outcome required, not an already verified property of the proposal.
Could both modes use wildcard slots and still make the same unsound assumption?

Yes. Equality between modes would not establish that the wildcard's scope reflects every heap slot permitted by the IR after a provenance-losing cast. Full-recompute comparison and semantic soundness remain different obligations. Defining the wildcard and its alias relationships against the documented semantics is necessary even if incremental and full runs agree.

The approach must still handle dependent recursive summaries, match full recomputation's alias answers after single-function edits, and meet the separate 50% median-latency goal; none of those outcomes is established by the proposal.

How should I understand ‘versioned SCC deltas’ at this stage?

Does replacing a coarse update with deltas mean recursive SCCs can be ignored?

Is a version change by itself enough to know which callers to update?

Could the proposed deltas cover removals as well as additions to possible alias targets?

Is parity just a comparison of how many aliases each mode reports?

Where does latency enter, and what is its comparator?

Latency is the performance dimension of the planned benchmark. Could we assume finer-grained propagation is faster without measuring it?

If the parity benchmark passes, could I skip the semantic-oracle check?

Could soundness and parity both pass while latency misses the target?

Does the plan specify which casts, opaque calls, or recursive programs go into the benchmark?

What would make the wildcard treatment unsound even if versioned propagation reached every caller?

I propose using generation-stamped dependency snapshots and SCC-local rebuilds for deleted call targets and shrinking summaries, so incremental updates avoid stale alias edges.

That proposal focuses on retraction: when an edit removes a possible indirect-call target or makes a function summary smaller, previously derived alias edges may no longer have support. A generation-stamped dependency snapshot could distinguish the dependencies used to derive an answer from those available after the edit. An SCC-local rebuild could then reconsider cyclic dependencies where simple removal may be insufficient. These are proposed mechanisms, not an implemented or measured result.
What makes this a different problem from propagating a newly possible call target?

With an added target, the analysis needs to account for new possible effects. With a deleted target, it may need to retract effects previously attributed to that target—but only if no other permitted target or dependency still supports them. Simply retaining all old edges could leave incremental answers different from full recomputation. Simply removing every edge associated with the deleted target could wrongly discard edges supported elsewhere.

No. The proposal refers to a target ceasing to be among the possible callees of a call. The call itself may still exist and have other possible targets. Whether a target is actually excluded must follow the edited program and the documented IR semantics; an update cannot declare a callee impossible solely because it disappeared from an incomplete cached list.
And what do you mean by a shrinking summary?

A function summary shrinks when it represents fewer alias-relevant possibilities or effects after an edit. For example, at a conceptual level, a possible effect could cease to be supported. That does not prescribe particular summary fields or assert that every edit makes a summary shrink. The proposal addresses the case where earlier caller reasoning depended on information the updated summary no longer contains.

A caller may summarize effects of functions an indirect call can reach. If one callee is no longer possible, effects supported only by that callee may cease to belong in the caller’s summary. Other callees or independent paths might still support the same effects, however. A deleted target is a reason to reconsider the summary, not proof that every associated alias edge must disappear.
What exactly is a stale alias edge?

Conceptually, it is a stored alias relationship or points-to consequence carried over from an earlier program state even though the edited program no longer supports it under the analysis’s rules. An edge can look stale after one dependency disappears yet remain justified by another. Avoiding stale edges therefore requires reconsidering their support, rather than deleting by association or retaining them indefinitely.

An extra edge may avoid an unsound exclusion, but it can still make incremental alias answers differ from full recomputation on the edited program. The broader goal requires those answers to match after single-function edits. Moreover, retaining unsupported edges can influence derived call targets and summaries. The proposal seeks to remove stale information while preserving every alias possibility the documented IR semantics still allow.

The proposal does not fix its granularity. Conceptually, a generation stamp distinguishes dependency information captured at one stage of analysis from information after an update.
